title: What the Fathers gave
hookLine: a way of reading scripture inside a praying Church

lines: NOW WITH PEOPLE WHO LIVED THERE.
cards: Open a Bible alone at the kitchen table and it can feel like walking into a huge house by yourself: rooms everywhere, doors you don't know how to open.
Now walk in again with people who lived there, who prayed in those rooms, argued over them, died rather than leave. Ignatius, Polycarp, Irenaeus. Athanasius and Basil.
Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome. John Chrysostom. Leo, Benedict, Gregory.
Today closes this first stretch of the year with one question: what did all of them leave behind? Today's word is Church Fathers.

teach.b: The Church Fathers are the teachers of the early centuries whom the Church trusts as witnesses to its faith: bishops, monks, a few laymen, and alongside them women like Macrina and Paula, whom you've met too.
What they left isn't mainly a set of answers. It's a way of reading. First, they read scripture as one story.
The Old Testament and the New were one book about one God, and Christ was the key that opened it.
Second, they read it inside the liturgy. Sermons like Leo's and Gregory's were preached at Mass, to people who had just heard the readings.
Scripture wasn't a private hobby; it was the Church's own voice, read aloud, then broken open like bread.
Third, they read it to love. Augustine wrote that anyone who thinks they've understood scripture, but whose reading doesn't build up love of God and neighbor, hasn't understood it yet.
And Gregory the Great said that the words of scripture grow with the one who reads them. Come back older, and the same verse is bigger.
Catholic teaching today says scripture is meant to be read within the living tradition of the whole Church, and the Fathers are a large part of what that means.
The Psalms put it simply, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." The Fathers carried that lamp a long time before handing it on.

how: Catholics meet the Church Fathers in the Office of Readings, where a passage from scripture is followed by a passage from a Father, and in homilies and catechesis that quote them.

practice: Let one name from this stretch come to mind, whichever surfaces first: Augustine's restless heart, Bede finishing, Leo walking out to meet Attila, Isidore, who said that when we read, God speaks.
Rest with that person for a moment, as if they were sitting beside you at the kitchen table. If you pray, thank God for the people who handed the lamp on.
